content: Larviciding involves the routine application of chemical or microbial insecticides to water bodies or containers to eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae, which are the aquatic immature stages of mosquitoes. The objective of this research was to evaluate whether larviciding with chemical or microbial insecticides can effectively prevent malaria transmission. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CAB Abstracts, LILACS, WHO ICTRP, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the ISRCTN registry, with the search completed on June 6, 2019. The studies included in the analysis were cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs), interrupted time series (ITS), randomized cross-over studies, non-randomized cross-over studies, and controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs) that compared larviciding interventions to no larviciding. The trials were independently assessed for eligibility and risk of bias, and data were extracted. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Four studies met the inclusion criteria: one cRCT, two CBAs, and one non-randomized cross-over study. All studies utilized ground application of larvicides, where individuals manually delivered the larvicides. One study evaluated chemical larvicides, while three focused on microbial agents. These studies were conducted in The Gambia, Tanzania, Kenya, and Sri Lanka. Three studies were conducted in areas with less extensive mosquito aquatic habitats (less than 1 km²), while one study was conducted in an area with more extensive habitats (greater than 1 km²). The latter was a cross-over study from The Gambia. In areas with aquatic habitats of less than 1 km²: A cRCT in Sri Lanka randomized eight villages to assess chemical larviciding using an insect growth regulator. This study found that larviciding was associated with a reduction in malaria incidence (rate ratio 0.24, 4649 participants, low-certainty evidence) and parasite prevalence (risk ratio 0.26, 5897 participants, low-certainty evidence) compared to no larviciding. Two CBA studies conducted in Kenya and Tanzania evaluated microbial larvicides. These studies reported a reduction in malaria prevalence during the intervention period (parasite prevalence risk ratio 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71 to 0.89; 70,902 participants; low-certainty evidence). The Kenyan study also reported a decrease in the incidence of new malaria cases (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.01; 720 participants; very low-certainty evidence). In areas with aquatic habitats of more than 1 km²: A non-randomized cross-over trial in The Gambia using microbial larvicides did not detect a significant effect on malaria incidence (risk ratio 1.58, 95% CI 0.94 to 2.65; 4226 participants) or parasite prevalence (risk ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.41 to 3.20; 3547 participants). Both outcomes were assessed as very low-certainty evidence. This trial also measured mean hemoglobin levels and found no significant differences across the four comparisons (mean difference –0.13, 95% CI –0.40 to 0.13; 3586 participants). Entomological outcomes could not be summarized or pooled due to missing or unreported data. In conclusion, most controlled studies on larviciding have utilized microbial agents. Ground larviciding appears to have some effect on malaria transmission in areas with non-extensive larval habitats. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine its effectiveness in large-scale aquatic habitats. Additionally, no studies were identified that used larviciding application techniques capable of covering large aquatic habitats, such as aerial spraying with aircraft.
